# HarborBuddy

HarborBuddy is a noncommercial source-available Go service for automatic container updates on a standalone Docker Engine. It compares image IDs, recreates eligible running containers, checks replacement readiness, and attempts rollback when replacement fails.

Maintainer: MikeO7 — https://github.com/MikeO7
Canonical website: https://mikeo7.github.io/HarborBuddy/
Source repository: https://github.com/MikeO7/HarborBuddy
License: PolyForm Noncommercial License 1.0.0; commercial use is not permitted by the current license.
Release status: early stage, with no versioned release yet. The `latest` and `edge` container tags currently follow `main`.

## Intended use

- Run continuously or as a one-shot command against one standalone Docker Engine.
- Check for new images on an interval or at a configured daily time.
- Recreate eligible running containers only when a pull resolves to a different image ID.
- Keep the stopped original container as a temporary backup until the replacement is ready.

## Update and rollback behavior

- HarborBuddy pulls the exact image reference stored in Docker and compares image IDs.
- It re-inspects a container before changing it to detect concurrent changes.
- The old container is stopped, disconnected, and renamed before the replacement starts, so updates are not zero-downtime.
- Optional rollback image retention is disabled by default. A positive `updates.rollback_image_retention` (or `HARBORBUDDY_ROLLBACK_IMAGE_RETENTION`) keeps that many prior known-working images per full image reference after successful readiness; retention failures are warnings and images referenced by running or stopped containers are not deliberately removed.
- With a Docker health check, readiness requires `healthy`. Without one, HarborBuddy checks that the process stays running without restarting for two seconds; this is not proof of application health.
- Creation, startup, or readiness failure triggers an attempted cleanup and restoration of the old container. Rollback is best-effort and can fail.
- Operator-supplied settings are retained where possible, while command, entrypoint, and health-check defaults inherited from the old image can move to the new image defaults.
- Docker Swarm tasks, auto-remove containers, container namespace dependencies, and inspected mounts that cannot be reproduced are skipped.
- HarborBuddy recreates from Docker inspection data. It does not invoke Docker Compose or reread a Compose file.

## Control and maintenance

- Eligible running containers are managed by default unless excluded by filters or `com.harborbuddy.autoupdate=false`.
- Image allow and deny patterns are supported; deny rules take precedence.
- Dry-run pulls images and changes the local image cache, but does not stop, recreate, rename, or remove containers and does not remove cleanup resources.
- Cleanup is enabled by default and deletes dangling images older than 24 hours.
- `HARBORBUDDY_CLEANUP_ALL=true` additionally enables stopped-container, unused-network, unused-volume, build-cache, and unused-tagged-image cleanup.
- Each broader cleanup category has an independent switch and defaults to off.
- For containers, networks, and volumes, cleanup age is measured from creation, not from when a resource became unused.
- System or in-use resources and resources with unknown age or usage are skipped. Volume cleanup can remove application data after the final container reference is gone.
- Logs use stable event names and correlated cycle IDs, with text or JSON output and optional rotating files.

## Automatic self-update

- Automatic self-update is enabled by default and can be disabled independently.
- A short-lived helper replaces the HarborBuddy daemon after the daemon exits.
- The helper keeps the old daemon as a backup until the new daemon passes startup readiness, then removes it.
- Self-update rollback is best-effort.
- `HARBORBUDDY_CONTAINER_NAME` should identify the daemon's stable container name and must be set explicitly for reliable remote-daemon self-identification.

## Security and integration boundaries

- HarborBuddy requires read/write Docker API access, which is equivalent to host-level administrative access.
- Run only one HarborBuddy controller per Docker daemon; this recommendation is not enforced.
- Remote Docker endpoints must use Docker's standard TLS environment variables and be reachable from the self-update helper.
- HarborBuddy sends no registry authentication with image pulls. Authenticated private-registry pulls are not currently supported.
- Published images target `linux/amd64`, `linux/arm64`, and `linux/arm/v7`.
